To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have improved the space-time tradeoffs for full-text indexing with one edit distance error.

for the case of an unbounded alphabet we have improved the space complexity by a logarithmic factor, and that for the case where the alphabet is bounded, we have improved the time complexity by a logarithm of the log of the size of the text.

for the problem of approximate full-text indexing with one edit error we can achieve: O(nlogε n) space and O(m+occ) time, for any ε∈(0,1), O(nloglog n) space and time O((m + occ) loglog n), and O(n) space and timeO(m+occ), for a constant alphabet.

our result is optimal in the sense of space-time trade-offs for constant alphabeted texts and optimal in the sense that it matches the lower bound of Chan and Lam for unbounded alphabets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for the problem of approximate full-text indexing with one edit error, we have improved in space and time both for an unbounded and for a constant alphabet.
for any constant ε, our results improve the space-time tradeoffs for this problem in all regimes of the parameters m and occ, with the only exception being when occ=o(mlogn).
we have shown that for both unbounded and constant alphabets, the space-time tradeoff curve for this problem has a linear region, and that the best known results are in that linear region.
The main takeaway from our work is that
compressed indices can be useful in obtaining space-time tradeoffs for full-text indices.
, by combining the ideas from the compressed indices with the techniques of Cole et  al., one can obtain improved results for approximate full-text indexing with one edit error.
compressed text indices can be used to obtain better space-time trade-offs than the previous results that were based on the use of succinct data structures.
